claim: Anesthesia is a major confounding factor in preclinical stroke research as stroke rarely occurs in sedated patients.
source: Anesthesia is a major confounding factor in preclinical stroke research as stroke rarely occurs in sedated patients.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical context of stroke and the limitations of preclinical models, drawing on established knowledge about when strokes typically occur in patients.

claim: Anesthesia affects both brain functions and the stroke outcome acting as neurotoxic or protective agents.
source: Moreover, anesthesia affects both brain functions and the stroke outcome acting as neurotoxic or protective agents.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to review articles cited later in the manuscript discussing anesthesia effects.

claim: No approaches were well suited to induce stroke while imaging hemodynamics along with simultaneous large-scale recording of brain functions in awake animals prior to this study.
source: So far, no approaches were well suited to induce stroke while imaging hemodynamics along with simultaneous large-scale recording of brain functions in awake animals.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of existing literature and methods, representing an inference from the state of the field.

claim: The first critical hours following the stroke insult and associated functional alteration remain poorly understood.
source: For this reason, the first critical hours following the stroke insult and associated functional alteration remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of existing methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Functional ultrasound (fUS) imaging was used to continuously monitor variations in cerebral blood volume (CBV) in +65 brain regions/hemispheres for up to 3 hr after stroke onset.
source: Functional ultrasound (fUS) imaging was used to continuously monitor variations in cerebral blood volume (CBV) in +65 brain regions/hemispheres for up to 3 hr after stroke onset.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental method and data collection performed in this study.

claim: Focal cortical ischemia was induced using a chemo-thrombotic agent suited for permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion in awake rats.
source: The focal cortical ischemia was induced using a chemo-thrombotic agent suited for permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion in awake rats and followed by ipsi- and contralesional whiskers stimulation to investigate on the dynamic of the thalamocortical functions.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: Early (0–3 hr) and delayed (day 5) fUS recording enabled characterization of the features of the ischemia (location, CBV loss), spreading depolarizations (occurrence, amplitude) and functional alteration of the somatosensory thalamocortical circuits.
source: Early (0–3 hr) and delayed (day 5) fUS recording enabled to characterize the features of the ischemia (location, CBV loss), spreading depolarizations (occurrence, amplitude) and functional alteration of the somatosensory thalamocortical circuits.
evidence: This summarizes the experimental findings from the study's data collection.

claim: Post-stroke thalamocortical functions were affected at both early and later time points (0–3 hr and 5 days) after stroke.
source: Post-stroke thalamocortical functions were affected at both early and later time points (0–3 hr and 5 days) after stroke.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the study.

claim: Preclinical stroke models suffer from several limitations that narrow the experimental focus on a few conditions when compared to clinics.
source: Indeed, when compared to clinics, preclinical stroke models suffer from several limitations that narrow the experimental focus on a few conditions (Macrae, 2011; Fluri et al., 2015; Sommer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature reviews.

claim: Most strokes occur in awake or sleeping patients but rarely in sedated patients.
source: As the first limitation, the use of anesthesia in preclinical studies seems to hamper the transition from animal to patient as most of stroke occurs in awake or sleeping patients (Mackey et al., 2011; Muir, 2023), but rarely in sedated patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Anesthetics disrupt brain functionality and alter neurovascular coupling.
source: Moreover, anesthetics disrupt the brain functionality, alters neurovascular coupling (Reimann and Niendorf, 2020; Masamoto and Kanno, 2012), while differentially affecting metabolism, electrophysiology, temperature, blood pressure, and tissue outcome by acting as neurotoxic or neuroprotective agents (see reviews Traystman, 2010; Hoffmann et al., 2016; Slupe and Kirsch, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Only a few groups succeeded in inducing a stroke in awake rodents.
source: To date, only a few groups succeeded in inducing a stroke in awake rodents (Seto et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Balbi et al., 2017; Sunil et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies that achieved this.

claim: Post-stroke network and functional alterations have been addressed by few preclinical studies, providing evidence of functional network reorganization from minutes to days following stroke onset.
source: Moreover, post-stroke network and functional alterations have been addressed by few preclinical studies, providing evidence of functional network reorganization from minutes (Mohajerani et al., 2011; Brunner et al., 2018) to days Dijkhuizen et al., 2001; Dijkhuizen et al., 2003; Abo et al., 2001; Weber et al., 2008; Shih et al., 2014 following stroke onset.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Previous studies mostly focused on cortical readouts and were unable to capture how deeper brain regions, like thalamic relays, were functionally and/or temporally affected remotely from the stroke insult.
source: However, these studies mostly focused on the cortical readouts and were unable to capture how deeper brain regions, like thalamic relays, were functionally and/or temporally affected remotely from the stroke insult (e.g. diaschisis) (Zhang et al., 2012; Carrera and Tononi, 2014; Cao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on review of previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies on post-stroke functional alterations were always conducted using various anesthetics known to differentially impact brain functions.
source: Furthermore, these studies were always conducted using various anesthetics (e.g. ventilated with halothane or isoflurane; medetomidine, urethane) known to differentially impact brain functions, as mentioned above.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of previous literature and established knowledge about anesthetics.

claim: Live monitoring of the hyperacute stroke-induced hemodynamics was restricted to few methods but often focused to the brain surface until recently.
source: Until recently, live monitoring of the hyperacute stroke-induced hemodynamics was restricted to few methods but often focused to the brain surface (Balbi et al., 2017; Levy et al., 2012; Dunn, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methods papers.

claim: fUS is a recent neuroimaging modality measuring cerebral blood volume changes (CBV).
source: On the other hand, fUS, a recent neuroimaging modality measuring cerebral blood volume changes (CBV) (Macé et al., 2011; Demené et al., 2019; Montaldo et al., 2022), was successfully employed to measure brain functions of awake rodents (Urban et al., 2015; Sieu et al., 2015; Macé et al., 2018; Bergel et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2021), to address early post-stroke functional reorganization (Brunner et al., 2018), and to track stroke-induced hemodynamics at the brain-wide scale (i.e. ischemia and spreading depolarization Brunner et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational fUS papers.

claim: fUS was successfully employed to measure brain functions of awake rodents.
source: On the other hand, fUS, a recent neuroimaging modality measuring cerebral blood volume changes (CBV) (Macé et al., 2011; Demené et al., 2019; Montaldo et al., 2022), was successfully employed to measure brain functions of awake rodents (Urban et al., 2015; Sieu et al., 2015; Macé et al., 2018; Bergel et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2021), to address early post-stroke functional reorganization (Brunner et al., 2018), and to track stroke-induced hemodynamics at the brain-wide scale (i.e. ischemia and spreading depolarization Brunner et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: fUS was used to address early post-stroke functional reorganization.
source: On the other hand, fUS, a recent neuroimaging modality measuring cerebral blood volume changes (CBV) (Macé et al., 2011; Demené et al., 2019; Montaldo et al., 2022), was successfully employed to measure brain functions of awake rodents (Urban et al., 2015; Sieu et al., 2015; Macé et al., 2018; Bergel et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2021), to address early post-stroke functional reorganization (Brunner et al., 2018), and to track stroke-induced hemodynamics at the brain-wide scale (i.e. ischemia and spreading depolarization Brunner et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: fUS was used to track stroke-induced hemodynamics at the brain-wide scale including ischemia and spreading depolarization.
source: On the other hand, fUS, a recent neuroimaging modality measuring cerebral blood volume changes (CBV) (Macé et al., 2011; Demené et al., 2019; Montaldo et al., 2022), was successfully employed to measure brain functions of awake rodents (Urban et al., 2015; Sieu et al., 2015; Macé et al., 2018; Bergel et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2021), to address early post-stroke functional reorganization (Brunner et al., 2018), and to track stroke-induced hemodynamics at the brain-wide scale (i.e. ischemia and spreading depolarization Brunner et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: No study has exploited fUS strategies to combine stroke hemodynamics and brain-wide functional alteration in awake rodents prior to this work.
source: However, no study has further exploited such strategies to combine stroke hemodynamics and brain-wide functional alteration in awake rodents.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of the literature.

claim: Rat #1 was excluded after the control session as the imaging window was too anterior to capture both cortical and thalamic responses.
source: Rat #1 was excluded after the control session as the imaging window was too anterior to capture both cortical and thalamic responses.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data and exclusion criteria.

claim: Rat #2 was excluded as hemodynamic responses were inconsistent during baseline (pre-stroke) period.
source: Rat #2 was excluded as hemodynamic responses were inconsistent during baseline (pre-stroke) period.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data and exclusion criteria.

claim: Rat #9 showed early post-stroke reperfusion and was excluded from stroke analysis.
source: Rat #9 showed early post-stroke reperfusion and was excluded from stroke analysis, the control session (pre-stroke) from Rat #9 was analyzed.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data and exclusion criteria.

claim: All imaging sessions started at approximately 8 am, aligning closely with the end of the rats' active phase.
source: All imaging sessions started at approximately 8 am, aligning closely with the end of their active phase.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental procedures.

claim: Each rat was subjected to two cranial windows accessing independently the distal branch of the left MCA and the selected brain regions to image.
source: Each rat was subjected to two cranial windows accessing independently the distal branch of the left MCA (Figure 1B, Left) and the selected brain regions to image (Figure 1B, Right).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, with reference to Figure 1B showing the cranial windows.

claim: The imaging window was performed between bregma –2 and –4 mm allowing for jointly monitoring the bilateral thalamocortical circuits of the somatosensory whisker-to-barrel pathway.
source: The latter was performed between bregma –2 and –4 mm allowing for jointly monitoring the bilateral thalamocortical circuits of the somatosensory whisker-to-barrel pathway, including the ventroposterior medial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM) and the primary somatosensory barrel-field cortex (S1BF).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and anatomical targeting.

claim: The selected coronal cross-section includes the posterior nucleus of the thalamus (Po), the reticular nucleus of the thalamus, and the ventral part of the zona incerta which are known for relaying information related to whiskers.
source: Moreover, the selected coronal cross-section includes the posterior nucleus of the thalamus (Po), the reticular nucleus of the thalamus, and the ventral part of the zona incerta are known for relaying information related to whiskers (Adibi, 2019; Bosman et al., 2011), and also direct efferent projections from the S1BF to other cortical and subcortical regions (Zakiewicz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim combines experimental design with established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rats were extensively trained to accept comfortable restraints in the experimental apparatus suitable for fUS recording of brain functions and stroke induction under awake conditions.
source: Prior to imaging sessions, rats were extensively trained to accept comfortable restraints in the experimental apparatus (Figure 1C), suitable for fUS recording of brain functions and stroke induction under awake conditions.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: After data acquisition, the coronal cross-section was registered and segmented on a custom-developed digital rat atlas to provide a dynamic view of the changes in perfusion.
source: After data acquisition, the coronal cross-section was registered and segmented on a custom-developed digital rat atlas (Brunner et al., 2022a) to provide a dynamic view of the changes in perfusion induced either by the stroke or evoked activity.
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure with citation to the atlas.

claim: The MCA was occluded by the means of a chemo-thrombotic ferric chloride solution (FeCl3).
source: To overcome the limitations of conventional stroke models, we occluded the distal branch of the MCA by the mean of a chemo-thrombotic ferric chloride solution (FeCl3) (Karatas et al., 2011; Syeara et al., 2020) while performing fUS imaging in awake rats (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure with citations to previous work using this method.

claim: The rats did not show any obvious signs of pain or discomfort during the restrain period and occlusion procedure.
source: It should be mentioned that the rats did not show any obvious signs of pain or discomfort (e.g. vocalization, aggressiveness) during the restrain period and occlusion procedure.
evidence: This is an observational report from the experimental procedure.

claim: The MCA occlusion (MCAo) was captured live with fUS and confirmed by the large drop of signal localized in the cortex of the left hemisphere.
source: The MCA occlusion (MCAo) was captured live with fUS and confirmed by the large drop of signal, i.e., ischemia, localized in the cortex of the left hemisphere (Figure 2B and C, Video 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) as shown with µDoppler image taken 3 hr and 5d after the stroke onset (dashed outline, Figure 2B, Top row).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to multiple figures and video.

claim: Bmode images accounting for the brain tissue echogenicity remain unchanged early after stroke onset (3 hr) while showing focal hyper-echogenicity lately after stroke onset (5d) as a marker of focal lesion.
source: Bmode images accounting for the brain tissue echogenicity remain unchanged early after stroke onset (3 hr) while showing focal hyper-echogenicity (dashed outline, Figure 2B, Bottom row) lately after stroke onset (5d) as a marker of focal lesion (Gómez-de Frutos et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to Figure 2B and citation to previous work on this imaging marker.

claim: The stroke-induced hemodynamic changes have been continuously recorded for up to 3 hr after stroke onset and registered and segmented into 69 regions.
source: The stroke-induced hemodynamic changes have been continuously recorded for up to 3 hr after stroke onset, registered and segmented into 69 regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collection procedure.

claim: There was an abrupt drop of rCBV down to ~40% of the baseline level after the occlusion of the MCA, followed by a progressive decrease of the rCBV to 30% of baseline level 3 hr after the stroke onset in the S1BF cortex of the left hemisphere.
source: We first extracted the average change in rCBV (∆rCBV in %) in the S1BF cortex of the left hemisphere (blue region, Figure 2B) and detected an abrupt drop of rCBV down to ~40% of the baseline level after the occlusion of the MCA, followed by a progressive decrease of the rCBV to 30% of baseline level 3 hr after the stroke onset (Figure 2C and Video 1).
evidence: This describes quantitative experimental findings with reference to figures and video.

claim: The signal extracted from the retrosplenial granular cortex (RSGc) shows successive and transient increases of signal characterizing hemodynamic events associated with spreading depolarizations (SDs) in the left hemisphere.
source: Second, we extracted the average rCBV change from a cortical region supplied by the anterior cerebral artery directly after the MCAo. The signal extracted from the retrosplenial granular cortex (RSGc; purple and black regions in Figure 2B) shows successive and transient increases of signal. It characterizes hemodynamic events associated with spreading depolarizations (SDs) in the left hemisphere (in purple; Figure 2D and Video 1) while resulting in a slight and stable oligemia in the right hemisphere (in black; Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to figures and video.

claim: SD events were observed in the peri-ischemic territory of all rats subjected to MCAo and occurred in an ostensibly random fashion.
source: SD events were observed in the peri-ischemic territory of all rats subjected to MCAo and occurred in an ostensibly random fashion (Figure 2E); however, hemodynamic events associated with SDs showed a similar bell shape and time-course across animals (Figure 2F).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to figures.

claim: Hemodynamic events associated with SDs showed a similar bell shape and time-course across animals.
source: SD events were observed in the peri-ischemic territory of all rats subjected to MCAo and occurred in an ostensibly random fashion (Figure 2E); however, hemodynamic events associated with SDs showed a similar bell shape and time-course across animals (Figure 2F).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: On average, five SD events per hour per rat were detected.
source: On average, we detected five SD events per hour per rat.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental findings.

claim: Brain slices stained 24 hr after MCAo confirmed that FeCl3-induced ischemia turned into tissue infarction.
source: Finally, we stained brain slices 24 hr after MCAo and confirmed that FeCl3-induced ischemia turned into tissue infarction (red delineation; Figure 2G).
evidence: This describes histological findings with reference to Figure 2G.

claim: Before stroke, the sensory-evoked stimulations elicited a robust and statistically significant functional response (z-score >1.6) for both left and right stimulation with the activity spatially confined in the contralateral dorsal part of the VPM and S1BF.
source: Before stroke, the sensory-evoked stimulations elicited a robust and statistically significant functional response (z-score >1.6, see Material and methods) for both left and right stimulation (orange and green, respectively; z-score maps; Pre-stroke panel, Figure 3B and Video 2) with the activity spatially confined in the contralateral dorsal part of the VPM and S1BF.
evidence: This describes experimental findings with statistical threshold and reference to figures and video.

claim: VPM, Po, and S1BF regions were significantly activated for both left and right stimuli before stroke (****p<0.0001, ***p<0.001 and ****p<0.0001, respectively).
source: The temporal analysis of the somatosensory evoked responses in the contralateral hemisphere confirmed that VPM, Po, and S1BF regions were significantly activated and for both left and right stimuli (****p<0.0001, ***p<0.001 and ****p<0.0001, respectively; Left panel, Figure 3C).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with statistical significance values and reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Significant increase of activity was detected in S2, AuD, Ect (****p<0.0001) and PRh (***p<0.001) cortices and VPL nucleus (**p<0.01) before stroke.
source: We also detected significant increase of activity in S2, AuD, Ect (****p<0.0001) and PRh (***p<0.001) cortices and VPL nucleus (**p<0.01; the list of acronyms is provided in Supplementary file 2), brain regions receiving direct efferent projections from the S1BF (Zakiewicz et al., 2014; Fabri and Burton, 1991; Frostig et al., 2008), VPM or Po nuclei (Viaene et al., 2011; El-Boustani et al., 2020; Landisman and Connors, 2007).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with statistical significance values and citations to anatomical connectivity studies.

claim: No habituation or sensitization due to the repetitiveness of whiskers stimulation was observed in cortical and subcortical regions over the pre-stroke sessions.
source: It is worth noted that no habituation or sensitization due to the repetitiveness of whiskers stimulation was observed in cortical and subcortical regions over the pre-stroke sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: After the stroke, the activity map from the left pad stimulation elicited a similar response pattern as pre-stroke.
source: After the stroke, the activity map from the left pad stimulation elicited a similar response pattern as pre-stroke; however, the right pad stimulation showed a total absence of functional response in the S1BF cortex and a significant reduction of the response in the VPM (z-score maps; Post-stroke panel, Figure 3B, and Video 2).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to figures and video.

claim: The right pad stimulation showed a total absence of functional response in the S1BF cortex and a significant reduction of the response in the VPM after stroke.
source: After the stroke, the activity map from the left pad stimulation elicited a similar response pattern as pre-stroke; however, the right pad stimulation showed a total absence of functional response in the S1BF cortex and a significant reduction of the response in the VPM (z-score maps; Post-stroke panel, Figure 3B, and Video 2).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to figures and video.

claim: Over the 3 hr following stroke onset, functional responses to left whisker stimulation were still detected in the cortical and thalamic regions of the contralateral (right) hemisphere.
source: Over the 3 hr following stroke onset, functional responses to left whisker stimulation were still detected in the cortical and thalamic regions of the contralateral (right) hemisphere; however, functional responses to right whisker stimulation were only detected in subcortical nuclei (i.e. VPM, Po, VPL), while attenuated when compared with the responses from the pre-stroke period and from the other hemisphere (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to figures.

claim: Functional responses to right whisker stimulation were only detected in subcortical nuclei (i.e. VPM, Po, VPL) over the 3 hr following stroke onset, while attenuated when compared with the responses from the pre-stroke period.
source: Over the 3 hr following stroke onset, functional responses to left whisker stimulation were still detected in the cortical and thalamic regions of the contralateral (right) hemisphere; however, functional responses to right whisker stimulation were only detected in subcortical nuclei (i.e. VPM, Po, VPL), while attenuated when compared with the responses from the pre-stroke period and from the other hemisphere (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to figures.

claim: No responses were detected at the cortical level (S1BF, S2, and AuD) for right whisker stimulation after stroke.
source: Furthermore, no responses were detected at the cortical level (S1BF, S2, and AuD; right panel, Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to figures.

claim: The hemodynamic responses before stroke were characterized by a quick increase in signal during whisker stimulation reaching a peak after 4.0 s at 18.2 ± 1.3% of baseline level for S1BF, 4.0 s at 4.6 ± 0.5% for VPM, and 2.4 s at 2.9 ± 0.7% for Po from the left stimulation.
source: Indeed, the hemodynamic responses were characterized by a quick increase in signal during whisker stimulation reaching a peak after 4.0 s at 18.2 ± 1.3% (4.0 s, 18.6 ± 1.2%) of baseline level for S1BF, 4.0 s at 4.6 ± 0.5% (3.2 s, 5.8 ± 0.7%) for VPM, and 2.4 s at 2.9 ± 0.7% (3.2 s, 4.0 ± 0.8%) for Po from the left stimulation (right, respectively; mean ±95% CI) before slowly returning to baseline level (black plots, Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes quantitative experimental findings with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: During the first hour following the stroke onset, functional responses in the left hemisphere (ipsilesional) were abolished in the S1BF, S2, and AuD (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ****p-value <0.0001).
source: During the first hour following the stroke onset, functional responses in the left hemisphere (i.e. ipsilesional) were abolished in the S1BF, S2, and AuD (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ****p-value <0.0001), significantly decreased in the VPM (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ***p-value <0.001), and unchanged in Po and VPL (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ns; Figure 3D) when compared with the pre-stroke responses (Pre-stroke, black plots, Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with statistical significance values and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: During the first hour following the stroke onset, functional responses in the left hemisphere were significantly decreased in the VPM (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ***p-value <0.001).
source: During the first hour following the stroke onset, functional responses in the left hemisphere (i.e. ipsilesional) were abolished in the S1BF, S2, and AuD (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ****p-value <0.0001), significantly decreased in the VPM (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ***p-value <0.001), and unchanged in Po and VPL (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ns; Figure 3D) when compared with the pre-stroke responses (Pre-stroke, black plots, Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with statistical significance values and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: During the first hour following the stroke onset, functional responses in the left hemisphere were unchanged in Po and VPL (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ns).
source: During the first hour following the stroke onset, functional responses in the left hemisphere (i.e. ipsilesional) were abolished in the S1BF, S2, and AuD (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ****p-value <0.0001), significantly decreased in the VPM (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ***p-value <0.001), and unchanged in Po and VPL (0–1 hr Post-stroke, ns; Figure 3D) when compared with the pre-stroke responses (Pre-stroke, black plots, Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with statistical significance values and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Over the two following hours (i.e. 1–2 hr and 2–3 hr Post-stroke), the hemodynamic responses captured in the ipsilesional regions remained similar as those detected during the first post-stroke hour.
source: Over the two following hours (i.e. 1–2 hr and 2–3 hr Post-stroke), the hemodynamic responses captured in these regions remained similar as those detected during the first post-stroke hour (green plots, Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The functional responses of S1BF and VPM in the right hemisphere (contralesional) were conserved during the first hour after the stroke onset (ns, 0–1 hr Post-stroke).
source: Regarding the right hemisphere (i.e. contralesional), the functional responses of S1BF and VPM were conserved during the first hour after the stroke onset (ns, 0–1 hr Post-stroke; orange plots, Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with statistical significance values and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: During the two following hours, signal changes in S1BF show a significant and progressive decrease of activity (1–2 hr Post-stroke **p-value <0.01, 2–3 hr Post-stroke ****p-value <0.0001) in the contralesional hemisphere.
source: During the two following hours, signal changes in S1BF show a significant and progressive decrease of activity (1–2 hr Post-stroke **p-value <0.01, 2–3 hr Post-stroke ****p-value <0.0001; orange plots, Figure 3D; Similar observations were made for S2 and AuD) whereas responses in VPM remained stable during the second hour post-stroke (1–2 hr, ns) before significantly decreasing during the third hour (2–3 hr Post-stroke *p-value <0.05; orange plots, Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with statistical significance values and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Responses in VPM in the contralesional hemisphere remained stable during the second hour post-stroke (1–2 hr, ns) before significantly decreasing during the third hour (2–3 hr Post-stroke *p-value <0.05).
source: During the two following hours, signal changes in S1BF show a significant and progressive decrease of activity (1–2 hr Post-stroke **p-value <0.01, 2–3 hr Post-stroke ****p-value <0.0001; orange plots, Figure 3D; Similar observations were made for S2 and AuD) whereas responses in VPM remained stable during the second hour post-stroke (1–2 hr, ns) before significantly decreasing during the third hour (2–3 hr Post-stroke *p-value <0.05; orange plots, Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with statistical significance values and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The functional responses in VPM and Po in the contralesional hemisphere remained unchanged over the 3 hr following the stroke onset.
source: Finally, the functional responses in VPM and Po remained unchanged over the 3 hr following the stroke onset (bottom panel, Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Two animals were imaged five days after the MCAo following the same experimental, stimulation, imaging, and processing conditions as for the early post-stroke session.
source: Two animals were imaged five days after the MCAo following the same experimental, stimulation, imaging, and processing conditions as for the early post-stroke session.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for the delayed imaging timepoint.

claim: Given that only two rats were imaged at the 5-day timepoint, the findings presented should be viewed as preliminary or proof of concept.
source: Given that only two rats were imaged at this timepoint, the findings presented here should be viewed as preliminary or proof of concept.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of the limitations of the data.

claim: Five days after the MCA occlusion, the ultrasound probe was positioned to find back the recording plane from Pre-Stroke session using Bmode and µDoppler imaging using brain vascular landmarks.
source: Five days after the MCA occlusion, we first placed the ultrasound probe over the imaging window and adjusted its position (using micromanipulator) to find back the recording plane from Pre-Stroke session using Bmode (morphological mode) and µDoppler imaging using brain vascular landmarks (i.e. vascular patterns, brain surface, and hippocampus Brunner et al., 2021; Brunner et al., 2023; see Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure with citations and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Functional responses to left whisker stimulation were still detected in the right hemisphere (contralesional) at the cortical and subcortical levels five days after stroke.
source: Functional responses to left whisker stimulation were still detected in the right hemisphere (i.e. contralesional), at the cortical and subcortical levels (orange; Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The functional responses to right whisker stimulation were only detected in the subcortical nuclei and not at the cortical level five days after stroke.
source: As for the early post-stroke imaging period, the functional responses to right whisker stimulation were only detected in the subcortical nuclei and not at the cortical level (green; Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The functional responses in the left S1BF 5 days after the stroke onset remained abolished when compared with the pre-stroke period, while slightly increased when compared with the 3 hr post-stroke timepoint.
source: At this later time point, the functional responses in the left S1BF (dark green plot, left panel, Figure 4B. Similar observations were made for the S2 and AuD) remained abolished when compared with the pre-stroke period (black plot), while slightly increased when compared with the 3 hr post-stroke timepoint (green plot).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The responses detected in the VPM 5d after the stroke onset were largely decreased when compared with the pre-stroke signal and with the 3 hr post-stroke trace.
source: The responses detected in the VPM 5d after the stroke onset (dark green plot, left panel, Figure 4B) were largely decreased not only when compared with the pre-stroke signal (black plot) but also with the 3 hr post-stroke trace (green plot).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Both the amplitude and time-to-peak of the hemodynamic response function in VPM were very similar to those from the early post-stroke signal (3 hr post-stroke); however, the post-peak period was largely dampened in the 5d post-stroke signal.
source: Interestingly, both the amplitude and time-to-peak of the hemodynamic response function were very similar to those from the early post-stroke signal (i.e. 3 hr post-stroke); however, the post-peak period was largely dampened in the 5d post-stroke signal.
evidence: This describes experimental findings comparing different timepoints.

claim: A similar alteration of the hemodynamic response function was observed for the 5d post-stroke signal extracted from the Po nucleus when compared to the pre-stroke and 3 hr post-stroke signals.
source: A similar alteration of the hemodynamic response function was also observed for the 5d post-stroke signal extracted from the Po nucleus when compared to the pre-stroke and 3 hr post-stroke signals (left panel, Figure 4B. Similar observations were made for the VPL).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The S1BF functional responses to left whisker stimulation in the right hemisphere were still reduced when compared with pre-stroke responses but remained like the traces detected at 3 hr post-stroke (non-significant) at 5 days post-stroke.
source: Regarding the right hemisphere (i.e. non-ischemic; right panel, Figure 4B), the S1BF functional responses to left whisker stimulation were still reduced when compared with pre-stroke responses (black plot) but remained like the traces detected at 3 hr post-stroke (orange plot, non-significant).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Both the amplitude and time-to-peak of the hemodynamic responses from the right VPM responses were consistent with pre-stroke and 3 hr post-stroke values but the post-peak signal was decreased at 5 days post-stroke.
source: As for the left VPM, both the amplitude and time-to-peak of the hemodynamic responses from the right VPM responses were consistent with pre-stroke and 3 hr post-stroke values but the post-peak signal was decreased (brown plot).
evidence: This describes experimental findings comparing different timepoints.

claim: The functional responses extracted from the Po and VPL in the right hemisphere did not show changes when compared to pre-stroke and 3 hr post-stroke responses at 5 days post-stroke.
source: The functional responses extracted from the Po and VPL did not show changes when compared to pre-stroke and 3 hr post-stroke responses.
evidence: This describes experimental findings comparing different timepoints.

claim: The FeCl3 model is well suited to study stroke under awake conditions compared to highly-invasive conventional strategies such as clipping or suturing.
source: Compared to highly-invasive conventional strategies such as clipping or suturing (Macrae, 2011; Fluri et al., 2015), the FeCl3 model used here, is well suited to study stroke under awake conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with other methods, supported by citations.

claim: The use of FeCl3 requires less manipulation, allows to maintain the dura intact, and strongly reduces the risk of hemorrhage and animal loss.
source: Indeed, the use of FeCl3 requires less manipulation, allows to maintain the dura intact, and strongly reduces the risk of hemorrhage (Karatas et al., 2011; Syeara et al., 2020) and animal loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work with the FeCl3 model.

claim: The FeCl3 model closely mimics key features of human stroke, including focal ischemia, clot formation, minutes-long progressive occlusion of the vessel, possibility of vessel recanalization, and penumbral tissue.
source: In addition, the FeCl3 model closely mimics key features of human stroke, including focal ischemia, clot formation, minutes-long progressive occlusion of the vessel, possibility of vessel recanalization, and penumbral tissue (Karatas et al., 2011; Syeara et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work characterizing the FeCl3 model.

claim: To adequately and efficiently occlude the vessel of interest with FeCl3, it is necessary to open the skull and to stabilize the cranial window under chronic conditions.
source: However, to adequately and efficiently occlude the vessel of interest, it is necessary to open the skull and to stabilize the cranial window under chronic conditions (i.e. case of delayed occlusion).
evidence: This is a description of the technical requirements of the method based on the authors' experience.

claim: Optimal preparation of the MCA window is highly critical, as the application of FeCl3 is performed with a reduced field-of-view.
source: It is worth noting that optimal preparation of the MCA window is highly critical, as the application of FeCl3 is performed with a reduced field-of-view.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' experimental experience.

claim: One rat was excluded from the analysis due to spontaneous MCA re-perfusion, thus reducing the success rate of the model.
source: In fact, as mentioned in the animal use report, one rat was excluded from the analysis due to spontaneous MCA re-perfusion, thus reducing the success rate of the model.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental outcomes.

claim: The FeCl3-induced MCAo showed an abrupt and massive drop of blood perfusion remaining constant during the entire recording period.
source: The FeCl3-induced MCAo showed an abrupt and massive drop of blood perfusion remaining constant during the entire recording period.
evidence: This describes experimental findings from the study.

claim: The ischemia was confined within the cortical territory perfused by the MCA, and the infarct (location and size) is in agreement with previous observations.
source: The ischemia was confined within the cortical territory perfused by the MCA (Figure 2B), and the infarct (location and size; Figure 2G) is in agreement with previous observations (Syeara et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2022a).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to figures and citations to previous work.

claim: Transient hyperemic events associated with spreading depolarizations (SDs) were detected within the peri-ischemic territory, with occurrence, frequency, and amplitude of the hemodynamic waves consistent with prior observation.
source: We also detected transient hyperemic events associated with spreading depolarizations (SDs) within the peri-ischemic territory, with occurrence, frequency, and amplitude of the hemodynamic waves (Figure 2D–F) consistent with prior observation (Brunner et al., 2022a; Nakamura et al., 2010; Takeda et al., 2011; Bere et al., 2014; Farkas et al., 2008; Farkas et al., 2010; Bogdanov et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with reference to figures and citations to previous work.

claim: The spatiotemporal dynamic of the FeCl3-induced MCAo is consistent with previous fUS imaging reports on cortical ischemia with various stroke models.
source: Moreover, the spatiotemporal dynamic of the FeCl3-induced MCAo is consistent with previous fUS imaging reports on cortical ischemia with various stroke models (Brunner et al., 2018; Brunner et al., 2022a; Hingot et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous fUS imaging studies.

claim: In the awake stroke experimental context, cerebral hemodynamics and functional responses to stimuli in rats remain stable over the hour-long imaging sessions.
source: In our awake stroke experimental context, cerebral hemodynamics and functional responses to stimuli in rats remain stable over the hour-long imaging sessions; however, we must mention the potential impact of such prolonged physical restraint on physiological and hemodynamic parameters (Nagasaka et al., 1980; Aydin et al., 2011; Sikora et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with acknowledgment of potential confounds supported by citations.

claim: One asset of the fUS imaging technology relies on its ability to track subtle hemodynamic changes in sparse brain regions.
source: On top of tracking large hemodynamic variation (i.e. ischemia, SDs), one asset of the fUS imaging technology relies on its ability to track subtle hemodynamic changes in sparse brain regions (Brunner et al., 2018; Macé et al., 2011; Urban et al., 2015; Macé et al., 2018; Brunner et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2021; Urban et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous fUS studies.

claim: Functional responses to mechanical whisker stimulation were detected in several regions relaying the information from the whisker to the cortex, including the VPM and Po nuclei of the thalamus, and S1BF.
source: Functional responses to mechanical whisker stimulation were detected in several regions relaying the information from the whisker to the cortex, including the VPM and Po nuclei of the thalamus, and S1BF, the somatosensory barrel-field cortex.
evidence: This describes experimental findings from the study.

claim: Responses were observed in the S2 cortex involved in the multisensory integration of the information.
source: Responses were also observed in the S2 cortex involved in the multisensory integration of the information (Adibi, 2019; Bosman et al., 2011; Lohse et al., 2021), the auditory cortex as it receives direct efferent projection from S1BF (Zakiewicz et al., 2014; Lohse et al., 2021), and the VPL nuclei of the thalamus are connected via corticothalamic projections (Zakiewicz et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with citations to anatomical and functional studies.

claim: The abrupt loss in S1BF responses after stroke was mainly driven by the focal ischemia.
source: While the abrupt loss in S1BF responses was mainly driven by the focal ischemia, the immediate but partial drop in VPM responses (Figure 3D) might result from the direct the loss of the excitatory corticothalamic feedback to the VPM (Landisman and Connors, 2007; Bourassa et al., 1995; Temereanca and Simons, 2004), or even from a dampening of thalamocortical excitability (Tennant et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The immediate but partial drop in VPM responses might result from the loss of the excitatory corticothalamic feedback to the VPM, or from a dampening of thalamocortical excitability.
source: While the abrupt loss in S1BF responses was mainly driven by the focal ischemia, the immediate but partial drop in VPM responses (Figure 3D) might result from the direct the loss of the excitatory corticothalamic feedback to the VPM (Landisman and Connors, 2007; Bourassa et al., 1995; Temereanca and Simons, 2004), or even from a dampening of thalamocortical excitability (Tennant et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The absence of cortical feedback suggests that the dampened functional responses might be driven by the intrinsic activity of the VPM in response to whisker stimulation.
source: The absence of such cortical feedback suggests that the dampened functional responses might be driven by the intrinsic activity of the VPM in response to whisker stimulation.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Five days after the initial injury, nuclei of the thalamus (VPM and Po) were subjected to a delayed and robust functional alteration, probably associated with diaschisis.
source: Five days after the initial injury, nuclei of the thalamus (VPM and Po) were subjected to a delayed and robust functional alteration (Figure 4B) as previously confirmed in other thalamic relay (Tokuno et al., 1992), probably associated with diaschisis, as previously characterized by tissue staining, reduction of metabolism, functions and perfusion (Zhang et al., 2012; Carrera and Tononi, 2014; Cao et al., 2020; Viaene et al., 2011; Tokuno et al., 1992).
evidence: This describes experimental findings with speculation about the mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The decrease in functional responses of the S1BF extracted from the right hemisphere (contralesional) shortly after the stroke onset could be provoked by a loss of transcortical excitability.
source: Functional responses of the S1BF extracted from the right hemisphere (i.e. contralesional) show a significant decrease shortly after the stroke onset (Figure 3D), and still detected at day 5, could be provoked by a loss of transcortical excitability (Rema and Ebner, 2003; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The late drop in VPM responses might be explained by corticothalamic modulation of the projections toward VPM.
source: The late drop in VPM responses might be explained by corticothalamic modulation of the projections toward VPM (Adibi, 2019; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The results obtained from awake head-fixed rats are in contradiction with a similar work showing higher contralesional responses to whisker stimulation during early stages of ischemic stroke.
source: While preliminary, these results obtained from awake head-fixed rats are in contradiction with a similar work by our group (fUS imaging, distal MCAo with microvascular clip, electrical whisker stimulation) showing higher contralesional responses to whisker stimulation during early stages of ischemic stroke (Brunner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The previous experiments were subjected to a long-term isoflurane regimen known to alter functional responses and disrupt hemodynamics.
source: However, these experiments were subjected to a long-term isoflurane regimen (surgery and imaging) known to alter functional responses (Sicard et al., 2006; Paasonen et al., 2016; Ayata et al., 2004) as well as disrupting hemodynamics (Martin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference about confounding factors in previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Further studies will be needed to accurately dissect the complex and long-lasting post-stroke alterations of the functional whisker-to-barrel pathway, including at the neuronal level by direct electrophysiology recordings and imaging.
source: Therefore, further studies will be needed to accurately dissect the complex and long-lasting post-stroke alterations of the functional whisker-to-barrel pathway, including at the neuronal level by direct electrophysiology recordings and imaging, as fUS only report on hemodynamics as a proxy of local neuronal activity (Sieu et al., 2015; Macé et al., 2018; Urban et al., 2014; Aydin et al., 2020; Sans-Dublanc et al., 2021; Nunez-Elizalde, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs, acknowledging limitations of the current method with citations.

claim: fUS only reports on hemodynamics as a proxy of local neuronal activity.
source: Therefore, further studies will be needed to accurately dissect the complex and long-lasting post-stroke alterations of the functional whisker-to-barrel pathway, including at the neuronal level by direct electrophysiology recordings and imaging, as fUS only report on hemodynamics as a proxy of local neuronal activity (Sieu et al., 2015; Macé et al., 2018; Urban et al., 2014; Aydin et al., 2020; Sans-Dublanc et al., 2021; Nunez-Elizalde, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of fUS measurements, supported by citations.

claim: The brain imaging paradigm was constrained to a single cross-section, thus missing out-of-plane brain regions also affected by the stroke or involved in the whisker network.
source: Another limitation relies on the experimental condition as our brain imaging paradigm was constrained to a single cross-section, thus missing out-of-plane brain regions also affected by the stroke (e.g. ischemic size, infract extension, origin, and propagation pattern of SDs)(Topchiy et al., 2009) or involved in the whisker network (e.g. superior colliculus, striatum, amygdala and cerebellum)(Adibi, 2019).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of experimental limitations with citations.

claim: One can extend the size of the cranial window to allow for larger scale imaging either by sequentially scanning the brain, or by using the recently developed volumetric fUS which provides whole-brain imaging capabilities.
source: To overcome such limitation, one can extend the size of the cranial window to allow for larger scale imaging either by sequentially scanning the brain (Sieu et al., 2015; Macé et al., 2018; Brunner et al., 2021; Brunner et al., 2023; Hingot et al., 2020; Sans-Dublanc et al., 2021; Brunner et al., 2017; Brunner et al., 2022b), or by using the recently developed volumetric fUS which provides whole-brain imaging capabilities in anesthetized rats (Rabut et al., 2019) and awake mice/rats (Brunner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work, supported by citations to relevant methods.

claim: This proof-of-concept work did not specifically focus on the impact of sex dimorphism, sleep/wake cycle on the stroke, or early behavioral outcomes following the insult.
source: Finally, it is important to note that this proof-of-concept work did not specifically focus on the impact of (i) sex dimorphism, (ii) sleep/wake cycle on the stroke, or (iii) early behavioral outcomes following the insult that would greatly enhance the translational value of such preclinical stroke study (Fisher et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations with citation to translational considerations.

claim: The brain-wide capability of fUS opens the door to investigate on stroke-affected brain circuits and functions using transgenic lines combined with opto-/chemo-genetic strategies.
source: Beyond studying the whisker-to-barrel somatosensory circuit, the brain-wide capability of fUS opens the door to investigate on stroke-affected brain circuits and functions using transgenic lines combined with opto-/chemo-genetic strategies as the technology is fully mature for mice studies (Macé et al., 2018; Brunner et al., 2020; Brunner et al., 2021; Sans-Dublanc et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about future research possibilities, supported by citations.

claim: The experimental procedures were approved by the Committee on Animal Care of the Katholieke Universiteit Leuven (ECD P172/2018).
source: The experimental procedures were approved by the Committee on Animal Care of the Katholieke Universiteit Leuven (ECD P172/2018), following the national guidelines on the use of laboratory animals and the European Union Directive for animal experiments (2010/63/EU).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats weighed between 250–400 g were used.
source: Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats weighed between 250–400 g (n=9; Janvier Labs, France) were used.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The body restraint and head fixation procedures are adapted from published protocols and setups dedicated to brain imaging of awake rats.
source: The body restraint and head fixation procedures are adapted from published protocols and setups dedicated to brain imaging of awake rats (Martin et al., 2006; Topchiy et al., 2009; Martin et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure with citations to previous methods.

claim: Rats were habituated to the workbench and to be restrained in a sling suit by progressively increasing restraining periods from minutes to hours for one or two weeks.
source: Rats were habituated to the workbench and to be restrained in a sling suit (Lomir Biomedical inc, Canada) by progressively increasing restraining periods from minutes (5 min, 10 min, 30 min) to hours (1 and 3 hr) for one or two weeks.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Habituation was completed when the rat remains still and calm over long restraint periods.
source: Habituation was completed when the rat remains still and calm over long restraint periods as previously established (Topchiy et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure with citation to previous work.

claim: A 1 mm cranial window was performed at coordinates bregma +2 mm and lateral 7 mm, over the left distal branch of the MCA.
source: After scalp removal and tissue cleaning, a 1 mm (Fluri et al., 2015) cranial window was performed at coordinates bregma +2 mm and lateral 7 mm, over the left distal branch of the MCA as reported in Brunner et al., 2018.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure with citations.

claim: A silicone plug was used to protect the window and ease the access to the MCA before the occlusion procedure.
source: A silicone plug (Body Double-Fast Set, Smooth-on, Inc, USA) was used to protect the window and ease the access to the MCA before the occlusion procedure.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure.

claim: A stainless-steel custom-designed headpost was fixed with bone screws and dental cement to the animal skull.
source: Then, a stainless-steel custom-designed headpost was fixed with bone screws (19010–00, FST, Germany) and dental cement (Super-Bond C&B, Sun Medical Co., Japan) to the animal skull (Figure 1B, left) as previously described by Brunner et al., 2020.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure with citation and reference to figure.

claim: A second cranial window was performed between bregma –2 to –4 mm and 6 mm apart from the sagittal suture after recovery and habituation to head-fixation.
source: After recovery and habituation to head-fixation, a second cranial window was performed between bregma –2 to –4 mm and 6 mm apart from the sagittal suture (same anesthesia settings as the first cranial window; see above) following the procedure described in Brunner et al., 2021; Figure 1B, right.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure with citation and reference to figure.

claim: This cranial window aims to cover bilateral thalamocortical circuits of the somatosensory whisker-to-barrel pathway.
source: This cranial window aims to cover bilateral thalamocortical circuits of the somatosensory whisker-to-barrel pathway.
evidence: This describes the purpose of the surgical procedure.

claim: For both cranial windows, the dura mater was kept intact.
source: For both cranial windows, the dura mater was kept intact.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure.

claim: Rats were medicated with analgesic (Buprenorphine, 0.1 mg/kg), anti-inflammatory (Dexamethasone, 0.5 mg/kg) drugs injected directly after the surgery, at 24 hr and 48 hr after the surgery.
source: Rats were medicated with analgesic (Buprenorphine, 0.1 mg/kg, Ceva, France), anti-inflammatory (Dexamethasone, 0.5 mg/kg, Dechra, Belgium) drugs injected directly after the surgery, at 24 hr and 48 hr after the surgery.
evidence: This describes the post-surgical care procedure.

claim: The mechanical fixation of the head-post ensures an easy and repeatable positioning of the ultrasound probes across imaging sessions.
source: The mechanical fixation of the head-post ensures an easy and repeatable positioning of the ultrasound probes across imaging sessions.
evidence: This describes a feature of the experimental setup.

claim: Brain landmarks (e.g. surface of the brain, hippocampus, superior sagittal sinus, large vessels) were used to find the plane of interest containing both S1BF and thalamic relays.
source: To find the plane of interest (containing both S1BF and thalamic relays: bregma - 3.4 mm), we used brain landmarks (e.g. surface of the brain, hippocampus, superior sagittal sinus, large vessels).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Two stimulation combs individually controlled by a stepper motor were used to deliver mechanical 5 Hz sinusoidal deflection of ~20° of amplitude for 5 s, alternatively to left and right whisker pads.
source: Two stimulation combs individually controlled by a stepper motor (RS Components, UK) were used to deliver mechanical 5 Hz sinusoidal deflection of ~20° of amplitude for 5 s, alternatively to left and right whisker pads.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimulation procedure.

claim: For each whisker pad, trials were spaced by a period of 1 min and 20 s without stimulation.
source: For each whisker pad, trials were spaced by a period of 1 min and 20 s without stimulation.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimulation procedure.

claim: The effective delay between two stimulations delivered to the same whisker pad is 80 s from start to start.
source: Thus, the effective delay between two stimulations delivered to the same whisker pad is 80 s from start to start.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental procedure.

claim: Coronal µDoppler images were acquired using a 15-MHz linear probe composed of 128 piezo-elements spaced by 100 µm connected to a dedicated ultrasound scanner.
source: Coronal µDoppler images were acquired using a 15-MHz linear probe composed of 128 piezo-elements spaced by 100 µm (L22-14Vx, Vermon, France) connected to a dedicated ultrasound scanner (Vantage 128, Verasonics, USA) and controlled by a high-performance computing workstation (fUSI-2, AUTC, Estonia).
evidence: This describes the imaging hardware used.

claim: This configuration allowed imaging of the brain vasculature with a resolution of 100 μm laterally, 110 μm in depth, and 300 μm in elevation.
source: This configuration allowed us to image the brain vasculature with a resolution of 100 μm laterally, 110 μm in depth, and 300 μm in elevation (Brunner et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the imaging resolution with citation.

claim: The ultrasound sequence generated by the software is adapted from previous work.
source: The ultrasound sequence generated by the software is adapted from Macé et al., 2018 and Brunner et al., 2021
evidence: This describes the imaging method with citations.

claim: Ultrafast images of the brain were generated using five tilted plane-waves (–6°, –3°, +0.5°, +3°, +6°).
source: Ultrafast images of the brain were generated using five tilted plane-waves (–6°, –3°, +0.5°, +3°, +6°).
evidence: This describes the imaging method.

claim: This process enables a continuous acquisition of power Doppler images at a frame rate of 1.25 Hz during several hours.
source: Overall, this process enables a continuous acquisition of power Doppler images at a frame rate of 1.25 Hz during several hours.
evidence: This describes the imaging capability.

claim: The fUS dataset was registered to a custom digital rat brain atlas using one coronal plane (bregma –3.4 mm) from the stereotaxic atlas of Paxinos, 2014.
source: We registered the fUS dataset to a custom digital rat brain atlas used in Brunner et al., 2023, using one coronal plane (bregma –3.4 mm) from the stereotaxic atlas of Paxinos, 2014.
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure with citations.

claim: The dataset was segmented into 69 anatomical regions/hemispheres of the reference atlas.
source: The dataset was segmented into 69 anatomical regions/hemispheres of the reference atlas (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure.

claim: Relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) was used to analyze ischemia, transient hemodynamic events associated with SDs and functional changes.
source: We used the relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV, expressed in % as compared to baseline) to analyze ischemia, transient hemodynamic events associated with SDs and functional changes.
evidence: This describes the data analysis approach.

claim: rCBV is defined as the signal in each voxel compared to its average level during the baseline period.
source: rCBV is defined as the signal in each voxel compared to its average level during the baseline period.
evidence: This is a definition of the measurement used.

claim: Hemodynamic events associated with SDs were defined as transient increase of rCBV signal (+25%) detected with a temporal delay of <10 frames (i.e. 8 s) between the two regions of interest.
source: Hemodynamic events associated with SDs were defined as transient increase of rCBV signal (+25%) detected with a temporal delay of <10 frames (i.e. 8 s) between the two regions of interest, validating both the hyperemia and spreading features of hemodynamic events associated with spreading depolarizations (Brunner et al., 2023; Bere et al., 2014; Ayata and Lauritzen, 2015; Binder et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the analysis criteria with citations.

claim: Only voxels with a z-score >1.6 were considered significantly activated (p<0.05 for a one-tailed test).
source: Only voxels with a z-score >1.6 were considered significantly activated (p<0.05 for a one-tailed test).
evidence: This describes the statistical threshold used.

claim: Activated brain regions were detected from hemodynamic response time-courses using GLM followed by t-test across animals.
source: Activated brain regions were detected from hemodynamic response time-courses using GLM followed by t-test across animals as proposed in Brunner, Grillet et al., (Brunner et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method with citation.

claim: AUC were compared and analyzed using a non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test corrected for multiple comparison using a Dunn's test.
source: AUC were compared and analyzed using a non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test corrected for multiple comparison using a Dunn's test.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.

claim: Rats were killed 24 hr after the occlusion for histological analysis of the infarcted tissue.
source: Rats were killed 24 hr after the occlusion for histological analysis of the infarcted tissue.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: 50 μm thick coronal brain sections across the MCA territory were sliced on a vibratome and analyzed using the cresyl violet staining procedure.
source: 50 μm thick coronal brain sections across the MCA territory were sliced on a vibratome (VT1000S, Leica Microsystems, Germany) and analyzed using the cresyl violet (Electron Microscopy Sciences, USA) staining procedure (see Open Lab Book for procedure).
evidence: This describes the histological procedure.
